title: The Friction You're Not Choosing
author: Breckenridge, Amanda
summary: Amanda Breckenridge argues that the leaders she coaches most often fail not from bad judgment but from choosing silence over 'healthy friction' — naming a hard truth early because it serves the outcome, not because you want to win an argument. She illustrates the pattern through three composite leaders, each protecting a different thing (permission, likability, legitimacy) by telling themselves the problem 'isn't their lane,' would seem 'rude,' or is 'probably nothing.' In each case, the leader eventually reframes the avoidance and speaks up directly but without turning the conversation into judgment of a person, and the result is a more collaborative rather than defensive exchange. The piece closes with three concrete practices — clarify the outcome you're avoiding in writing, use existing meeting routines rather than staging a special confrontation, and state facts plainly without softening them into meaninglessness — arguing that the leaders who move their teams forward have simply decided silence costs more than speaking up.
points: Distinguishes healthy friction (naming a hard truth early to serve the outcome) from the friction people dread (delayed, defensive, score-settling).

Identifies three specific self-protective excuses for staying silent — 'not my lane,' fear of seeming rude, fear of overreacting — and what each is really protecting (permission, likability, legitimacy).
The costs of silence are invisible in the moment because they build gradually and surface later as distance, resentment, or a badly timed comment.
Recommends embedding hard conversations inside routines you already run (one-on-ones, standing meetings) rather than staging a separate, harder-to-schedule confrontation.
Argues intent, not directness, is what determines whether the same blunt words land as help or as an attack.
quotes: Healthy friction is one of the highest leverage choices a leader can make. Yet most people don't make it. Even though they see what's at stake, protecting how they're perceived feels safer than doing what's more useful.
A delay left unaddressed erodes results over time, as it did with Miriam's pipeline. A poorly defined role turns into underperformance that gets blamed on the person instead of the job.
She posted this in Slack: "This affects my numbers even though it isn't my org. Here's what I'm seeing, and here's what I need from this partnership going forward.
He named the issue without turning it into a judgment. The conversation became collaborative instead of defensive because he stayed focused on improving the work, not evaluating the person.
Every one of these excuses offers immediate relief. And every one of them also hands the problem to your future self.

Speak early, while the problem is still small and the conversation is easier to have. It can be the difference between a hard quarter and a lost one, between a role that gets fixed and a person who gets blamed for it, between a relationship that deepens and one that quietly cools.
